chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
title: Giving the audience your best: 'the old school'
summary: Dance contrasts Ellington and Hines, who felt they owed the audience a show, with later musicians who felt the audience owed them. Humes says she is from the old school and always does her best.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah, it's very nice. You know, maybe there's a difference between musicians that have come up in their earlier days and musicians in their later days because you know how it is; later on people, as there is more emphasis on art and so on. Alot of times people don't look at, I mean it's the same way, for instance Ellington and others like him always felt
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

that they owed the audience something. That they were giving to the audience; they owed them a performance, a good performance and their best personality and that there shouldn't be any limits. In other words, you give. And that was a professional pride in that. Well Earl Hines is the same too. But then later musicians figured that the audience owed them something for their art. But I think you . . .
You know, I just think if you're going to work, do the best you can and that's what I try to do each time I go out there.
